title: 50% of long COVID patients show improvement in 3 years — but the condition tends to linger in those with this subtype
summary: About half of people with long COVID see meaningful improvement in their symptoms after three years, a new study found.
body: Symptoms of long COVID ease in half of patients within three years of the infection that kicked off their illness. That's the primary conclusion of a new study that tracked over 1,000 patients with long COVID, a chronic condition that can emerge after an infection with the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Among the patients, the chance of improvement varied sharply depending on how the condition affected their bodily systems. In the study, published Tuesday (Nov. 3) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine , roughly 60% of patients whose predominant symptoms were changes to their ability to taste or smell had significantly improved three years after their first positive test. But less than 20% of those with a multisystem presentation had improved in that time frame. This latter group had symptoms that affected their cardiac, nervous and gastrointestinal systems, among others. An expert told Live Science that the condition resembled myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), which often arises after an infection and similarly impacts a wide range of bodily systems. The new study's findings could help direct the structure of future clinical trials of treatments for long COVID, …

title: One-third of babies diagnosed with peanut allergy don't actually have one, study hints
summary: New findings suggest that "food challenges" can help prevent children from being saddled with unnecessary allergy diagnoses.
body: A peanut allergy diagnosis in infancy can mean years of avoiding the food or undergoing treatments to build tolerance. But a recent study suggests that more than one-third of babies thought to have the allergy may stop reacting badly to peanuts within months of that diagnosis. In an analysis published in The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology: In Practice , researchers conducted supervised "food challenges" with infants diagnosed with a peanut allergy. These challenges involved giving the babies increasing amounts of peanut protein, with the intention of confirming whether they indeed had an allergy. The team found that more than 1 in 3 infants who underwent the food challenge tolerated the peanut protein, meaning they didn't experience symptoms of an allergic reaction. "This rate is much higher than we thought," study co-author Dr. Timothy Brettig , a pediatric allergist at the National Allergy Centre of Excellence in Australia, told Live Science. title: This self-powered toothbrush makes electricity to kill cavity-causing bacteria
summary: Researchers have created a self-charging toothbrush that helps fight the bacteria linked to cavities and gum disease while preventing plaque buildup.
body: A toothbrush that generates its own electricity with every stroke could offer a new way to fight the microbes behind cavities and gum disease. Conventional toothbrushes rely on physical scrubbing to remove plaque from teeth and gums. But even after a thorough brush, some bacteria remain and begin rebuilding plaque. To solve that problem, researchers have developed a self-powered toothbrush that converts the friction of brushing into an electrical charge. That electricity is intended to zap the plaque-promoting bacteria and keep them from colonizing teeth. "It's great to have new approaches that actually enhance the effect of mechanical cleaning," said Nicholas Jakubovics , an oral microbiologist at Newcastle University in the U.K. who was not involved in the study. "The idea that the toothbrush surface itself is actively doing something is really interesting." The experimental brush has bristles made from polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), a plastic that generates electricity when bent; these types of energy-producing materials are called piezoelectric. As the bristles flex during brushing, they produce an electrical charge that then triggers chemical reactions in saliva and water. T…

title: Mom experienced 'extreme unhappiness' only when she breastfed
summary: A new mom experienced intense feelings of sadness whenever she breastfed.
body: The patient: A woman in upstate New York The symptoms: About two weeks after her baby's birth, the woman began experiencing intensely negative emotions at every breastfeeding session. These feelings of "extreme unhappiness" would start just before her milk ejection reflex (during which milk moves from the breast ducts to the nipples) and last up to two minutes. The feelings would end abruptly when she finished breastfeeding and then appear again the next time she was about to release milk, according to a report of the case , which the patient co-authored. The patient was a breastfeeding counselor for the United States Department of Agriculture Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) Program. Until the baby was about 18 months old, this phenomenon would happen every time the woman breastfed — about five times per day, on average. Unlike postpartum depression ,‬ which can cause persistent feelings of despondency, anxiety and mood swings in new parents,‬ the woman felt "helpless, hopeless, [and] worthless" only during her milk release. title: Would you risk your health to visit Mars?
summary: A recent rat study hinted that cosmic radiation could pose health risks for future Mars explorers. Live Science asks its readers whether they'd take the journey anyway.
body: A crewed mission to Mars could be one of humanity's greatest achievements, but getting there may come with serious health risks. Beyond the challenges of surviving in space for months at a time, astronauts would face prolonged exposure to cosmic radiation ‪—‬ high-energy particles in space that can penetrate the human body and potentially damage vital organs. title: Nearly 30% of US adults admit to lying about or exaggerating their symptoms to get antibiotics from doctors, survey finds
summary: In two new surveys, U.S. adults report lying to their doctors and their children's doctors about symptoms in hopes of being prescribed antibiotics.
body: Nearly 30% of U.S. adults have lied to doctors in an effort to obtain antibiotics, either by exaggerating their actual symptoms or by fabricating symptoms, the results of a new national survey suggest. Additionally, in a second survey, about one-quarter of children's caregivers reported lying about their kids' symptoms to get antibiotics on their behalf. "As clinicians, we know that patients lie to us sometimes," Dr. Jeffrey Linder , a general internist and primary care clinician-investigator at Northwestern Medicine, wrote in a commentary about the survey findings . However, the results are still important because the inappropriate use of antibiotics can contribute to the mounting problem of antibiotic resistance , in which bacteria build up a tolerance to the drugs designed to kill them. Recent data released by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) highlight the extent of the problem: In 2023, drug-resistant bacteria and fungi caused about 9.7 million infections in the U.S., up from 2.8 million in 2017 . In turn, the estimated number of deaths caused by drug-resistant germs rose from 35,000 to 50,800 between the two years. A major factor driving resistance among b…

title: Study reveals new clues to why colorectal cancer in young people is so deadly
summary: Colorectal cancer in young people shows genetic and structural differences that may make it more aggressive and treatment-resistant than the cancer tends to be in older people.
body: Colorectal cancer rates have been rising in people under 50 since the mid-1990s. These early-onset cancers tend to be more aggressive and resistant to treatment than cancers in older adults — and now, scientists may be learning why. A new study published Thursday (Oct. 29) in the journal Nature Medicine compared colorectal tumors from people between 29 and over 90 years old, and it revealed key differences between young and old patients. The new findings might, in turn, help scientists uncover new ways to fight colorectal cancer in young people, said study co-author Ana Anderson , a professor of neurology at Harvard Medical School and a core faculty member of the Gene Lay Institute of Immunology and Inflammation at Brigham and Women's Hospital. "I believe that our study is essentially a turning point now in the field," Anderson told Live Science. "Because up until now, we've had more questions than answers." Many questions surround early-onset colorectal cancer, as the disease is rising in people under 50 even as it falls in older populations.
